outputs.L1: The invention relates to a scanning probe microscopy system for mapping nanostructures on a sample surface. The system is configured to sense a high-aspect-ratio nanostructure comprising at least one face having a slope angle, relative to the sample surface, that exceeds a predetermined threshold angle. The system comprises a metrology frame; a sample support structure for supporting a sample; and a sensor head including a probe, the probe comprising a cantilever and a probe tip. The scanning probe microscopy system further comprises an actuator configured to scan the probe tip relative to the substrate surface to map the nanostructures. To sense the high-aspect-ratio nanostructure, the probe tip is arranged at a fixed offset angle with respect to the sensor head so as to be angled relative to the sample surface. The system further comprises a sensor head carrier configured to receive the sensor head. The sensor head carrier and the sensor head are provided with mutually cooperating mounting structures that form a kinematic mount having at least three contact points for detachably mounting the sensor head on the sensor head carrier.
outputs.L2: The invention concerns a scanning probe microscopy apparatus configured to map nanostructures present on a sample surface. In particular, the apparatus can detect a high-aspect-ratio nanostructure having at least one face whose inclination, measured relative to the sample surface, is greater than a predefined threshold angle. The apparatus includes a metrology frame, a support structure for holding the sample, and a sensor head equipped with a probe comprising a cantilever and a probe tip. An actuator moves the probe tip in a scanning motion relative to the substrate surface to map the nanostructures. To detect the high-aspect-ratio structure, the probe tip is positioned at a fixed angular offset with respect to the sensor head, thereby orienting the tip at an angle to the sample surface. The apparatus also includes a carrier that receives the sensor head. Complementary mounting features on the carrier and sensor head together establish a kinematic mount with at least three contact points, allowing the sensor head to be detachably secured to the carrier.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a scanning probe microscopy system configured to map nanostructures on a sample surface. In particular, the system is designed to detect and characterize high-aspect-ratio nanostructures having at least one face with a slope greater than a predetermined threshold angle.

The system comprises a metrology frame, a sample support structure for holding the sample, and a sensor head. The sensor head includes a cantilever-based probe provided with a probe tip. An actuator produces relative scanning movement between the probe tip and the sample surface, thereby enabling the probe tip to trace and measure surface features.

To improve the detection of steep or substantially vertical nanostructure features, the probe tip is held at a fixed offset angle relative to the sample surface during scanning. This angled arrangement allows the probe to access and sense faces that might be difficult to measure using a conventionally oriented probe.

The sensor head is detachably coupled to a carrier by means of a kinematic mount. The kinematic mount includes at least three contact points, providing a stable, precise, and repeatable positioning interface while allowing the sensor head to be removed or replaced when required.
outputs.L4:
The scanning probe microscopy system is designed to characterize nanostructures having high aspect ratios, steep sidewalls, recessed surfaces, or other features that are difficult to access with a conventional vertically oriented probe. The system includes a probe tip mounted at a predetermined angle relative to the primary scanning or surface-normal direction. A scanning actuator moves the probe with respect to a sample, or moves the sample with respect to the probe, so that the tip can traverse selected regions of the nanostructure and generate measurement data representative of surface position, profile, roughness, or other nanoscale characteristics.

By maintaining a fixed lateral or angular offset between the probe tip and the actuator axis, the system allows the sensing portion of the tip to contact or otherwise interact with steeply sloped and substantially vertical faces. This geometry reduces interference between the probe body and the structure being measured, enabling access to sidewalls, trenches, pillars, and similarly challenging features. Signals produced during scanning may be processed to reconstruct a two-dimensional profile or a three-dimensional map of the measured structure.

The probe and associated sensing components are carried by a detachable sensor head. The sensor head is removably coupled to a carrier through a three-point kinematic mount. The three contact locations constrain the sensor head in a defined position and orientation while avoiding the uncertainty and mechanical stress that can result from an overconstrained attachment. A releasable retaining mechanism may hold the mating surfaces together during operation while permitting the sensor head to be removed for probe replacement, maintenance, calibration, or exchange with another sensor configuration.

When the sensor head is reinstalled, the kinematic mount returns it to substantially the same spatial position relative to the carrier and scanning actuator. This repeatable registration preserves the known probe offset and minimizes the need for realignment or recalibration after removal. Together, the angled probe geometry, controlled scanning motion, and repeatable three-point mounting arrangement provide reliable access to complex nanostructures and support accurate, reproducible nanoscale metrology.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest and most frequently used words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, “a book” can mean any book, while “the book” refers to a particular one.

Although it is easy to overlook, “the” plays an essential role in communication. It adds clarity, creates shared understanding, and helps listeners or readers recognize what is being discussed. This simple three-letter word shows how even the smallest parts of language can have a significant impact.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for sensing steep-sided nanoscale structures on a sample surface with an SPM probe fixed at an offset angle, including the metrology frame, sample support, actuator, sensor head carrier, and three-point kinematic mounting arrangement.
counterfactuals.output:
An apparatus for measuring steep-sided nanoscale features comprises a rigid **metrology frame** that defines a stable reference between a sample and an SPM sensor. A **sample support**, mounted to the frame, holds the sample with its nominal surface plane in a known orientation. A precision **actuator**, such as an XYZ piezoelectric stage, produces controlled relative motion between the sample and the sensor for scanning and probe approach.

The **sensor head** is secured to a removable carrier and holds an SPM probe—such as an AFM cantilever—at a fixed, nonzero offset angle relative to the sample-surface normal. The angled probe can therefore access and sense near-vertical or re-entrant sidewalls that a normally oriented probe cannot measure reliably.

The sensor-head carrier is coupled to the metrology frame by a **three-point kinematic mounting arrangement**. Three spaced contact interfaces, for example a cone, a V-groove, and a flat engaged by corresponding balls, constrain all six rigid-body degrees of freedom without overconstraint. Magnetic, spring, or other preload retains the carrier against the contacts. This arrangement permits rapid removal and replacement of the sensor head while reproducibly restoring the probe’s position and offset angle. Different carriers may provide opposite or selected probe inclinations, allowing multiple faces of steep nanoscale structures to be measured in a common metrology coordinate system.
